name: Camellia japonica extract
lead: Camellia japonica extract is derived from the Japanese camellia, a flowering evergreen tree or shrub; its leaves can be made into tea and are reported to contain anti-inflammatory terpenoids such as lupeol and squalene.[1] It is used in some cosmetics as a botanical ingredient, and Korean patent filings from 2004 and 2005 describe cosmetic compositions using it for anti-ageing, whitening and anti-inflammatory purposes.[2][3]
Evidence is thin: a 2025 study in hairless mice reported that topical extract reduced atopic-dermatitis-like signs.[4] No human studies were found.

paras: In the 2025 mouse study, four weeks of topical Camellia japonica extract reduced epidermal thickness and mast cell infiltration in a chemically induced atopic dermatitis model.[4] The patent filings claim moisturising, whitening and elasticity effects but are not clinical evidence.[2][3]

card.summary: Japanese camellia botanical used in some cosmetics, with one mouse study and no human data.
card.note: Only animal and patent material found.

quick.overview:
An extract from the Japanese camellia shrub, used in some cosmetics.

The only published research found is a 2025 mouse study; no human studies exist in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: In mice, topical extract reduced skin inflammation markers in an atopic dermatitis model.
quick.risks: No safety data for human cosmetic use were found.
